claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection for 48 hr induced caspase-3 activation in immortalized simian kidney epithelial Vero CCL81 cell lines.
source: Agreeing with previous reports (Chu et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2020), infection with SARS-CoV-2 for 48 hr induced caspase-3 and caspase-8 activation in immortalized simian kidney epithelial Vero CCL81 (Figure 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A (immunoblot) and is corroborated by citations to previous reports.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection for 48 hr induced caspase-8 activation in immortalized simian kidney epithelial Vero CCL81 cell lines.
source: Agreeing with previous reports (Chu et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2020), infection with SARS-CoV-2 for 48 hr induced caspase-3 and caspase-8 activation in immortalized simian kidney epithelial Vero CCL81 (Figure 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A (immunoblot) and is corroborated by citations to previous reports.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection for 48 hr induced caspase-3 activation in human lung epithelial Calu-3 cell lines.
source: Agreeing with previous reports (Chu et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2020), infection with SARS-CoV-2 for 48 hr induced caspase-3 and caspase-8 activation in immortalized simian kidney epithelial Vero CCL81 (Figure 1A) and human lung epithelial Calu-3 cell lines (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B and is corroborated by citations to previous reports.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection for 48 hr induced caspase-8 activation in human lung epithelial Calu-3 cell lines.
source: Agreeing with previous reports (Chu et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2020), infection with SARS-CoV-2 for 48 hr induced caspase-3 and caspase-8 activation in immortalized simian kidney epithelial Vero CCL81 (Figure 1A) and human lung epithelial Calu-3 cell lines (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and is corroborated by citations to previous reports.

claim: Features consistent with the predominance of apoptotic cell death were observed at 48 hr post-infection by flow cytometric analysis of annexin V and permeability dye co-staining in SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
source: We also found features consistent with the predominance of AC death at 48 hr post-infection by flow cytometric analysis of the pattern of annexin V and a permeability dye co-staining in infected cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C using flow cytometry.

claim: Low levels of cytolysis were observed in SARS-CoV-2 infected cells at 48 hr post-infection, as assessed by lactate dehydrogenase release.
source: Consistently, we observed low levels of cytolysis in these infected cells, as assessed by lactate dehydrogenase release (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D measuring LDH release.

claim: Immunofluorescent labeling of cleaved caspase-3 in lung tissues of deceased COVID-19 patients confirmed the induction of apoptosis in the epithelia infected with replicant SARS-CoV-2.
source: Immunofluorescent labeling of cleaved caspase-3 in lung tissues of deceased COVID-19 patients confirmed the induction of apoptosis in the epithelia infected with replicant SARS-CoV-2 (Figure 1E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from patient lung tissues shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Examination of lung tissues revealed evidence of macrophages with internalized epithelial cells and SARS-CoV-2, suggesting the uptake of infected epithelial cells by macrophages.
source: Examination of lung tissues also revealed evidence of macrophages with internalized epithelial cells and SARS-CoV-2, suggesting the uptake of infected epithelial cells by macrophages (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological examination data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Viral particles obtained from isolated apoptotic Vero cells induced cytopathic effect to an equivalent extent as those released in the culture supernatants.
source: We performed the median tissue culture infection dose (TCID50) assay and found that viral particles obtained from isolated apoptotic Vero and Calu-3 cells induced cytopathic effect to an equivalent extent as those released in the culture supernatants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by TCID50 assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Viral particles obtained from isolated apoptotic Calu-3 cells induced cytopathic effect to an equivalent extent as those released in the culture supernatants.
source: We performed the median tissue culture infection dose (TCID50) assay and found that viral particles obtained from isolated apoptotic Vero and Calu-3 cells induced cytopathic effect to an equivalent extent as those released in the culture supernatants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by TCID50 assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Annexin V-labeled apoptotic cells isolated from SARS-CoV-2-infected cell culture carry viable viral particles.
source: Furthermore, we isolated annexin V-labeled AC from SARS-CoV-2-infected cell culture and confirmed that they carry viable viral particles (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by TCID50 quantification data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Viable SARS-CoV-2 is retained within infected, apoptotic epithelial cells.
source: Therefore, viable SARS-CoV-2 is retained within infected, apoptotic epithelial cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing viral particles in isolated apoptotic cells.

claim: Exposure of phosphatidylserine on the outer plasma membrane of cells undergoing regulated cell death is the most ubiquitous signal that triggers their phagocytosis.
source: Exposure of phosphatidylserine (PtdSer) on the outer plasma membrane of cells undergoing regulated cell death, as observed by annexin V binding to infected dying cells (Figure 1C), is the most ubiquitous signal that triggers their phagocytosis (Fadok et al., 1992; Nagata, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature (Fadok et al., 1992; Nagata, 2018) and is consistent with scientific knowledge.

claim: Macrophages efficiently engulf SARS-CoV-2-infected apoptotic cells, similarly to the uptake of sterile, UV-irradiated apoptotic cells.
source: We observed that macrophages efficiently engulf CoV2-AC, similarly to the uptake of sterile, UV-irradiated AC (UV-AC) (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Analysis by confocal microscopy and staining for Spike protein confirmed the presence of SARS-CoV-2 in engulfed cell corpses.
source: Analysis by confocal microscopy and staining for Spike protein confirmed the presence of SARS-CoV-2 in engulfed cell corpses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Stimulation with infected or sterile dying cells did not robustly affect macrophages viability up to 24 hr post-treatment.
source: Finally, either stimulation with infected or sterile dying cells did not robustly affect macrophages viability up to 24 hr post-treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Macrophages engulf cell corpses carrying viable particles of SARS-CoV-2.
source: These results demonstrate that macrophages engulf cell corpses carrying viable particles of SARS-CoV-2, offering a framework to investigate their effects on macrophage function.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding section.

claim: The uptake of sterile apoptotic cells often promotes macrophage functional polarization toward an anti-inflammatory and tissue repair phenotype.
source: The uptake of sterile AC often promotes macrophage functional polarization toward an anti-inflammatory and tissue repair phenotype (Doran et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature (Doran et al., 2020).

claim: Stimulation of primary monocyte-derived macrophages with CoV2-AC, but not infection with SARS-CoV-2, reduced the expression of genes associated with alternative programming to tissue remodeling and secretion of immune-modulatory mediators such as CCL18, CD206 (also known as MRC1), MMP9, PPARG, and CD163.
source: We first observed that stimulation of primary monocyte-derived macrophages with CoV2-AC, but not infection with SARS-CoV-2, reduced the expression of genes associated with alternative programming to tissue remodeling and secretion of immune-modulatory mediators such as CCL18, CD206 (also known as MRC1), MMP9, PPARG, and CD163 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR gene expression data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Stimulation with UV-AC obtained from infected Vero cells increased both gene and surface protein expression of the anti-inflammatory marker CD206.
source: Furthermore, stimulation with UV-AC obtained from infected Vero cells increased both gene (Figure 2A) and surface protein (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) expression of the anti-inflammatory marker CD206.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Upregulation of MRC1 at the gene or protein levels did not occur in response to stimulation with CoV2-AC.
source: However, upregulation of MRC1 at the gene or protein levels did not occur in response to stimulation with CoV2-AC (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Similar results were obtained in THP-1-derived macrophages stimulated with CoV2-AC obtained from either Calu-3 or Vero cells infected with SARS-CoV-2.
source: We obtained similar results in THP-1-derived macrophages stimulated with CoV2-AC obtained from either Calu-3 or Vero cells infected with SARS-CoV-2 (Figure 2—figure supplement Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Stimulation with the conditioned supernatants of infected dying cells or direct infection with SARS-CoV-2 did not induce MRC1 transcription in macrophages.
source: Stimulation with the conditioned supernatants of infected dying cells (containing putative DAMP, cytokines produced by epithelial cells, extracellular vesicles, and released virions) or direct infection with SARS-CoV-2 did not induce MRC1 transcription (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) or surface expression (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D) in macrophages.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Stimulation with the conditioned supernatants of infected dying cells or direct infection with SARS-CoV-2 did not induce CD206 surface expression in macrophages.
source: Stimulation with the conditioned supernatants of infected dying cells (containing putative DAMP, cytokines produced by epithelial cells, extracellular vesicles, and released virions) or direct infection with SARS-CoV-2 did not induce MRC1 transcription (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) or surface expression (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D) in macrophages.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Modulation of CD206 expression occurred specifically in the macrophages that engulfed apoptotic cells and was not due to paracrine signaling.
source: We also confirmed that modulation of CD206 expression occurred specifically in the macrophages that engulfed AC and was not due to paracrine signaling (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Macrophages treated with epithelial apoptotic cells containing inactivated SARS-CoV-2 exhibited increased CD206 surface expression, similar to that of UV-AC.
source: Notably, macrophages treated with epithelial AC containing inactivated SARS-CoV-2 exhibited increased CD206 surface expression, similar to that of UV-AC (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Viable SARS-CoV-2 actively represses alternative programming carried in dying cells and is not primarily enforced by the type of cell death caused by the infection.
source: This finding suggests that viable SARS-CoV-2 actively represses alternative programming carried in dying cells and is not primarily enforced by the type of cell death caused by the infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that UV-inactivated virus in apoptotic cells does not suppress CD206 expression.

claim: Efferocytosis of sterile UV-AC in the presence of SARS-CoV-2 still induced higher expression of CD206 in macrophages.
source: Efferocytosis of sterile UV-AC in the presence of SARS-CoV-2 still induced higher expression of CD206 in macrophages (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The suppression of CD206 surface expression required delivery of viral particles within cell corpses to macrophages.
source: Therefore, the suppression of CD206 surface expression required delivery of viral particles within cell corpses to macrophages.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that virus must be within apoptotic cells to suppress CD206 expression.

claim: Sensing and engulfment of dying cells carrying viable SARS-CoV-2 switch macrophage anti-inflammatory, resolutive programming in response to efferocytosis toward an inflammatory phenotype.
source: Collectively, these findings support that sensing and engulfment of dying cells carrying viable SARS-CoV-2 switch macrophage anti-inflammatory, resolutive programming in response to efferocytosis toward an inflammatory phenotype.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding section.

claim: The uptake of CoV2-AC, but not UV-AC, significantly increased IL6 expression in monocyte-derived macrophages.
source: Conversely, the uptake of CoV2-AC, but not UV-AC, significantly increased IL6 expression in monocyte- and THP-1-derived macrophages (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The uptake of CoV2-AC, but not UV-AC, significantly increased IL6 expression in THP-1-derived macrophages.
source: Conversely, the uptake of CoV2-AC, but not UV-AC, significantly increased IL6 expression in monocyte- and THP-1-derived macrophages (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The uptake of CoV2-AC induced robust secretion of inflammatory IL-6 in primary macrophages.
source: The uptake of CoV2-AC also induced robust secretion of inflammatory IL-6 and IL-1β, in both primary (Figure 3B) and THP-1-derived macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytokine quantification data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The uptake of CoV2-AC induced robust secretion of inflammatory IL-1β in primary macrophages.
source: The uptake of CoV2-AC also induced robust secretion of inflammatory IL-6 and IL-1β, in both primary (Figure 3B) and THP-1-derived macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytokine quantification data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The uptake of CoV2-AC induced robust secretion of inflammatory IL-6 in THP-1-derived macrophages.
source: The uptake of CoV2-AC also induced robust secretion of inflammatory IL-6 and IL-1β, in both primary (Figure 3B) and THP-1-derived macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytokine quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The uptake of CoV2-AC induced robust secretion of inflammatory IL-1β in THP-1-derived macrophages.
source: The uptake of CoV2-AC also induced robust secretion of inflammatory IL-6 and IL-1β, in both primary (Figure 3B) and THP-1-derived macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cytokine quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: IL-6 and IL-1β were not detected in macrophages stimulated with the cell-free conditioned supernatants, and therefore this effect was not due to immune mediators or viral particles released from infected epithelial cells.
source: We did not detect these cytokines in macrophages stimulated with the cell-free conditioned supernatants (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C), and therefore this effect was not due to immune mediators or viral particles released from infected epithelial cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by cytokine quantification data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Assessment of IL-6 secretion in macrophages stimulated with sorted out populations of infected dying cells revealed that cytokine production occurred specifically in response to apoptotic cells, but not permeabilized dead cells.
source: Importantly, assessment of IL-6 secretion in macrophages stimulated with sorted out populations of infected dying cells revealed that cytokine production occurred specifically in response to AC, but not permeabilized dead cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CoV2-AC obtained from epithelial cells infected in the presence of osmoprotectant glycine still induced robust secretion of IL-6 by macrophages.
source: In agreement, CoV2-AC obtained from epithelial cells infected in the presence of osmoprotectant glycine, which non-specifically prevents the leak of cytosolic content by lytic permeabilization (Frank et al., 2000; Evavold et al., 2018) still induced robust secretion of IL-6 by macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and is consistent with the mechanism described in cited literature.

claim: The induction of inflammatory cytokines by SARS-CoV-2-loaded corpses required the presence of viable viral particles, as UV treatment or paraformaldehyde fixation of isolated CoV2-AC abrogated IL-6 secretion.
source: Further, the induction of inflammatory cytokines by SARS-CoV-2-loaded corpses required the presence of viable viral particles, as UV treatment or paraformaldehyde (PFA) fixation of isolated CoV2-AC abrogated IL-6 secretion (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Robust production of IL-6 was not observed in response to dying epithelial cells infected with Coxsackievirus.
source: Notably, we did not observe robust production of IL-6 in response to dying epithelial cells infected with Coxsackievirus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Augmented pro-inflammatory cytokine production is not a universal response of macrophages to the uptake of cell corpses infected with positive single-strand viruses.
source: This result suggests that augmented pro-inflammatory cytokine production is not a universal response of macrophages to the uptake of cell corpses infected with positive single-strand viruses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data comparing responses to SARS-CoV-2 and Coxsackievirus infected apoptotic cells.

claim: In the absence of PtdSer ligation, macrophages did not secrete IL-6 in response to CoV2-AC.
source: To confirm the requirement of recognition and binding of CoV2-AC to promote inflammatory skewing, we stimulated macrophages in the presence of annexin V to mask PtdSer exposed on the surface of the AC. In the absence of PtdSer ligation, macrophages did not secrete IL-6 in response to CoV2-AC (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Stimulation of macrophages in the presence of actin depolymerization inducer Cytochalasin D, which allows corpse binding but not internalization, attenuated IL-6 production.
source: Stimulation of macrophages in the presence of actin depolymerization inducer Cytochalasin D, which allows corpse binding but not internalization, also attenuated IL-6 production (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Remdesivir treatment of primary macrophages following stimulation with CoV2-AC partially reduced IL-6 secretion, suggesting that viral sgRNA expression is important to modulate the inflammatory response.
source: Finally, we tested the effect of antiviral drugs targeting viral RNA transcription (RdRP-mediated RNA synthesis). We found that Remdesivir treatment of primary macrophages following stimulation with CoV2-AC partially reduced IL-6 secretion, suggesting that viral sgRNA expression is important to modulate the inflammatory response (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3H and involves inference about the mechanism.

claim: The exacerbated cytokine production observed in response to the efferocytosis of infected cell corpses by macrophages may contribute to the cytokine storm associated with COVID-19 hyperinflammatory syndrome.
source: The exacerbated cytokine production observed in response to the efferocytosis of infected cell corpses by macrophages may contribute to the cytokine storm associated with COVID-19 hyperinflammatory syndrome.
evidence: The claim is speculative, connecting the experimental findings to a potential clinical manifestation.

claim: Engulfment of CoV2-AC by primary macrophages reduced the transcription of PtdSer receptors, including the scavenger receptors CD36 and SRA1, αVβ5 integrin (ITGB5), and T cell immunoglobulin mucin receptor 4 (TIM4) and MER proto-oncogene tyrosine kinase (MERTK).
source: We found that engulfment of CoV2-AC by primary macrophages reduced the transcription of such PtdSer receptors, including the scavenger receptors CD36 and SRA1, αVβ5 integrin (ITGB5), and T cell immunoglobulin mucin receptor 4 (TIM4) and MER proto-oncogene tyrosine kinase (MERTK) (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In THP-1-macrophages, reduced expression of SRA1, ITGB5, and TIM4 receptors was observed in response to infection with SARS-CoV-2.
source: In THP-1-macrophages, we also observed reduced expression of SRA1, ITGB5, and TIM4 receptors in response to infection with SARS-CoV-2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The engulfment of SARS-CoV-2-infected corpses suppressed the efferocytosis of other apoptotic cells.
source: To determine if repression of efferocytic receptors affects additional uptake of dying cells, we treated macrophages with CoV2-AC and subsequently fed them with apoptotic human Jurkat cells (UV-Jurkat). We found that the engulfment of SARS-CoV-2-infected corpses suppressed the efferocytosis of other AC (Figure 4B–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Infection with SARS-CoV-2 reduced apoptotic cell clearance to a lower extent than prior uptake of CoV2-AC.
source: As infection with SARS-CoV-2 reduced the expression of some efferocytic receptors in THP-1 macrophages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), we also tested if it affected the uptake of AC. Comparatively, infection with SARS-CoV-2 reduced AC clearance to a lower extent than prior uptake of CoV2-AC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Treatment with Remdesivir did not improve the subsequent uptake by macrophages stimulated with CoV2-AC, arguing that viral RNA replication is not required for suppression of efferocytosis in response to CoV2-AC.
source: Notably, treatment with Remdesivir did not improve the subsequent uptake by macrophages stimulated with CoV2-AC, arguing that viral RNA replication is not required for suppression of efferocytosis in response to CoV2-AC (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F and involves inference about the mechanism.

claim: Different mechanisms lead to pro-inflammatory cytokine production and efferocytosis repression in response to the uptake of infected corpses.
source: This result also suggests that different mechanisms lead to pro-inflammatory cytokine production and efferocytosis repression in response to the uptake of infected corpses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential effects of Remdesivir on cytokine production versus efferocytosis.

claim: Efferocytosis of SARS-CoV-2-infected dying cells affects the expression of efferocytic receptors and impairs the continual removal of apoptotic cells by macrophages.
source: Thus, efferocytosis of SARS-CoV-2-infected dying cells affects the expression of efferocytic receptors and impairs the continual removal of AC by macrophages.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding section.

claim: A reduction in the protein levels of CD36 was found in S1009+ infiltrating phagocytes in the lungs of COVID-19 patients compared to control tissues.
source: We found a reduction in the protein levels of CD36 in S1009+ infiltrating phagocytes in the lungs of COVID-19 patients compared to control tissues (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from patient lung tissues shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Phagocytes in the lungs of COVID-19 patients expressed lower protein levels of MERTK.
source: Phagocytes in the lungs of COVID-19 patients also expressed lower protein levels of MERTK (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from patient lung tissues shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Independent analysis of clusters previously assigned as macrophages revealed significant repression of gene sets related to efferocytosis in severe COVID-19 patients.
source: Independent analysis of clusters previously assigned as macrophages (Liao et al., 2020) revealed significant repression of gene sets related to efferocytosis in severe patients (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Differences in efferocytosis-related gene expression were evident between moderate and severe COVID-19 patients in clusters expressing markers of early infiltrating phagocytes (S1009+ CCL18-).
source: While differences were evident between moderate and severe patients in clusters expressing markers of early infiltrating phagocytes (S1009+ CCL18-), they were more pronounced in mature, likely anti-inflammatory macrophages (S11009- CCL18+).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis of scRNA-seq data.

claim: Differences in efferocytosis-related gene expression were more pronounced in mature, likely anti-inflammatory macrophages (S11009- CCL18+) compared to early infiltrating phagocytes.
source: While differences were evident between moderate and severe patients in clusters expressing markers of early infiltrating phagocytes (S1009+ CCL18-), they were more pronounced in mature, likely anti-inflammatory macrophages (S11009- CCL18+).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis of scRNA-seq data.

claim: Reassessment on scRNAseq by Ren et al., 2021 showed enrichment in pathways related to efferocytosis for genes repressed in alveolar macrophages which were positive for SARS-CoV-2 RNA compared with those which were negative for the virus.
source: Notably, reassessment on scRNAseq by Ren et al., 2021 showed enrichment in pathways related to efferocytosis for genes repressed in alveolar macrophages which were positive for SARS-CoV-2 RNA compared with those which were negative for the virus (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D and cites the source of the data.

claim: Uptake of infected cells reduces the capacity of macrophages to clear other dead cells.
source: This finding is consistent with the notion that uptake of infected cells reduces the capacity of macrophages to clear other dead cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the scRNA-seq analysis showing reduced efferocytosis gene expression in virus-positive macrophages.

claim: Macrophages in the lungs of severe COVID-19 patients may fail in their efferocytic capacity.
source: Altogether, these data support that macrophages in the lungs of severe COVID-19 patients may also fail in their efferocytic capacity.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the histological and scRNA-seq data presented.

claim: The sensing and engulfment of SARS-CoV-2-infected dying cells by macrophages switch the effector response to efferocytosis from a potential wound healing, anti-inflammatory function to a pro-inflammatory one.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the sensing and engulfment of SARS-CoV-2-infected dying cells by macrophages switch the effector response to efferocytosis from a potential wound healing, anti-inflammatory function to a pro-inflammatory one.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The uptake of cell corpses infected with SARS-CoV-2 exacerbates the secretion of inflammatory IL-6 and IL-1β.
source: Our data supports that the uptake of cell corpses infected with SARS-CoV-2 exacerbates the secretion of inflammatory IL-6 and IL-1β, suggesting a mechanism for the robust secretion of cytokines related to COVID-19 cytokine storm.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on cytokine secretion and involves speculation about clinical relevance.

claim: Efferocytosis of infected cells may augment tissue damage by causing inefficient clearance of dead cells.
source: Instead, our data suggest that efferocytosis of infected cells may augment tissue damage by causing inefficient clearance of dead cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing impaired continual efferocytosis.

claim: Inefficient clearance of dead cells may contribute to respiratory complications developed by patients with the severe form of COVID-19.
source: This process may consequently contribute to respiratory complications developed by patients with the severe form of the disease and increase susceptibility to secondary bacterial infections for the lack of effective disease tolerance mechanisms that restrain collateral tissue damage (Jamieson et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is speculative, connecting the experimental findings to potential clinical outcomes, with support from a citation.

claim: Inefficient clearance of dead cells may increase susceptibility to secondary bacterial infections for the lack of effective disease tolerance mechanisms that restrain collateral tissue damage.
source: This process may consequently contribute to respiratory complications developed by patients with the severe form of the disease and increase susceptibility to secondary bacterial infections for the lack of effective disease tolerance mechanisms that restrain collateral tissue damage (Jamieson et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is speculative, connecting the experimental findings to potential clinical outcomes, with support from a citation.

claim: The efferocytic capacity of lung monocytes and macrophages is compromised in severe COVID-19 patients.
source: We also provide evidence supporting that lung monocytes and macrophages from severe COVID-19 patients have compromised efferocytic capacity.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological and scRNA-seq data from patient samples.

claim: Dysfunctional efferocytosis of SARS-CoV-2-infected cell corpses suppresses macrophage anti-inflammation and efficient tissue repair programs.
source: Our findings reveal that dysfunctional efferocytosis of SARS-CoV-2-infected cell corpses suppresses macrophage anti-inflammation and efficient tissue repair programs and provides mechanistic insights for the excessive production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and accumulation of tissue damage associated with COVID-19 immunopathogenesis.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Dysfunctional efferocytosis of SARS-CoV-2-infected cell corpses provides mechanistic insights for the excessive production of pro-inflammatory cytokines associated with COVID-19 immunopathogenesis.
source: Our findings reveal that dysfunctional efferocytosis of SARS-CoV-2-infected cell corpses suppresses macrophage anti-inflammation and efficient tissue repair programs and provides mechanistic insights for the excessive production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and accumulation of tissue damage associated with COVID-19 immunopathogenesis.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Dysfunctional efferocytosis of SARS-CoV-2-infected cell corpses provides mechanistic insights for the accumulation of tissue damage associated with COVID-19 immunopathogenesis.
source: Our findings reveal that dysfunctional efferocytosis of SARS-CoV-2-infected cell corpses suppresses macrophage anti-inflammation and efficient tissue repair programs and provides mechanistic insights for the excessive production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and accumulation of tissue damage associated with COVID-19 immunopathogenesis.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Patients with severe and critical COVID-19 progress from pneumonia to development of acute respiratory distress syndrome and respiratory failure, septic shock, and multiorgan dysfunction.
source: Patients with severe and critical COVID-19 progress from pneumonia to development of acute respiratory distress syndrome and respiratory failure, septic shock, and multiorgan dysfunction (Siddiqi and Mehra, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Severe clinical manifestations of COVID-19 are caused by dysregulated host immune response, including compromised function of the myeloid compartment.
source: These severe clinical manifestations of the disease are caused by dysregulated host immune response, including compromised function of the myeloid compartment (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Lucas et al., 2020; Rodrigues et al., 2021; Schulte-Schrepping et al., 2020; Silvin et al., 2020; Valle et al., 2020; Veras et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Hyperinflammation and extensive unresolved tissue damage associated with dysfunctional innate responses should contribute to the pathogenesis of inflammatory lung disease and worsening of COVID-19.
source: Therefore, hyperinflammation and extensive unresolved tissue damage associated with dysfunctional innate responses should contribute to the pathogenesis of inflammatory lung disease and worsening of COVID-19, although underlying mechanisms are still loosely defined.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the cited literature and represents a logical conclusion, though mechanisms are not fully established.

claim: Macrophages and monocytes are functionally plastic cells that can promote homeostasis and resolution of inflammation by sensing microbial and host-derived signals and programming their gene expression toward an anti-inflammatory, pro-resolution, and wound-healing phenotype.
source: Macrophages and monocytes are functionally plastic cells that can promote homeostasis and resolution of inflammation by sensing microbial and host-derived signals and programming their gene expression toward an anti-inflammatory, pro-resolution, and wound-healing phenotype (Martins et al., 2019; Trzebanski and Jung, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature and represents scientific knowledge.

claim: Host-protective programming of macrophages reduces inflammatory cytokine production by other immune and non-immune cells and promotes the repair of damaged tissue to sustain physiological function and re-establish homeostasis.
source: This host-protective programming reduces inflammatory cytokine production by other immune and non-immune cells and promotes the repair of damaged tissue to sustain physiological function and re-establish homeostasis (Murray and Wynn, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature and represents scientific knowledge.

claim: The efficient clearance of dying cells prevents further tissue dysfunction caused by uncontrolled cytotoxicity and the release of damage-associated molecular patterns.
source: During the repair process, the efficient clearance of dying cells prevents further tissue dysfunction caused by uncontrolled cytotoxicity and the release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMP).
evidence: The claim represents established scientific knowledge about the role of efferocytosis.

claim: Defects in sensing, ingesting, and degradation of dead and dying cells through efferocytosis cause chronic inflammation and autoimmune diseases.
source: Defects in sensing, ingesting, and degradation of dead and dying cells through efferocytosis cause chronic inflammation and autoimmune diseases (Boada-Romero et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature and represents scientific knowledge.

claim: Efferocytosis couples corpse internalization to other environmental cues (such as local cytokines and metabolites) to temporally and spatially regulate macrophage anti-inflammatory and tissue repair functions.
source: In addition to preventing the deleterious effects of secondary necrosis, efferocytosis also couples corpse internalization to other environmental cues (such as local cytokines and metabolites) to temporally and spatially regulate macrophage anti-inflammatory and tissue repair functions (A-Gonzalez et al., 2017; Bosurgi et al., 2017; Perry et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature and represents scientific knowledge.

claim: While the clearance of apoptotic cells is often associated with alternative macrophage programming, the identity of the dying cell, the type of cell death, and the context of death (either sterile or infectious) can modulate the nature of the macrophage response.
source: While the clearance of apoptotic cells (AC) is often associated with alternative macrophage programming, the identity of the dying cell, the type of cell death, and the context of death (either sterile or infectious) can modulate the nature of the macrophage response (Rothlin et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established literature and represents scientific knowledge.

claim: Inhibition of apoptosis ameliorates cytokine expression and tissue damage in the lungs of SARS-CoV-2-infected mice, indicating that apoptosis in the lungs is pathogenic.
source: Notably, inhibition of apoptosis ameliorates cytokine expression and tissue damage in the lungs of SARS-CoV-2-infected mice, indicating that apoptosis in the lungs is pathogenic (Chu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Excessive amounts of necrotic cells may lead to high levels of circulating DAMP, such as HMGB1 and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), both of which correlate with disease severity in COVID-19.
source: In the context of COVID-19 immunopathogenesis, excessive amounts of necrotic cells may lead to high levels of circulating DAMP, such as HMGB1 and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), both of which correlate with disease severity (Chen et al., 2020; Han et al., 2020; Rodrigues et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing correlation between DAMP levels and disease severity.

claim: The combination of exacerbated cytokine production and interruption of continual efferocytosis in response to engulfment of SARS-CoV-2-infected corpses could both increase the magnitude and duration of inflammation, contributing to the hyperinflammatory state and multiorgan damage in COVID-19.
source: It is thus possible that the combination of exacerbated cytokine production and interruption of continual efferocytosis in response to engulfment of SARS-CoV-2-infected corpses could both increase the magnitude and duration of inflammation, contributing to the hyperinflammatory state and multiorgan damage in COVID-19.
evidence: The claim is speculative, connecting the experimental findings to potential clinical outcomes.

claim: Some studies reported higher levels of autoantibodies (such as against IFNγ, phospholipids, and annexin A2) in COVID-19 patients.
source: Finally, some studies reported higher levels of autoantibodies (such as against IFNγ, phospholipids, and annexin A2) in COVID-19 patients (Bastard et al., 2020; Zuniga et al., 2021; Zuo et al., 2020), suggesting that autoantibodies may drive the worsening of the disease.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies reporting autoantibodies in COVID-19 patients.

claim: Defective engulfment or processing of dying cells causes the development of autoimmune diseases.
source: It has long been known that defective engulfment or processing of dying cells causes the development of autoimmune diseases (Boada-Romero et al., 2020; Cohen et al., 2002; Miyanishi et al., 2007; Peng and Elkon, 2011; Rodriguez-Manzanet et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature and represents scientific knowledge.

claim: Defective clearance of apoptotic cells caused by SARS-CoV-2 infection and SARS-CoV-2-loaded ACs may contribute to COVID-19-associated autoimmunity.
source: In light of our findings, perhaps defective clearance of AC caused by SARS-CoV-2 infection and SARS-CoV-2-loaded ACs also contributes to COVID-19-associated autoimmunity.
evidence: The claim is speculative, connecting the experimental findings to potential clinical outcomes.

claim: Antivirals and other therapeutic efforts to limit viral replication may fail to benefit critically ill COVID-19 patients.
source: As it becomes clear that worsening of COVID-19 occurs because of immune dysfunction, antivirals, and other therapeutic efforts to limit viral replication may fail to benefit critically ill patients.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the understanding that immune dysfunction drives severe disease.

claim: Successful therapeutic strategies for critically ill COVID-19 patients may rely on targeting dysregulated components of the host response to limit damage to the host, thus promoting disease tolerance and stimulating a resolutive response that restores homeostasis.
source: In those patients, successful therapeutic strategies may rely on targeting dysregulated components of the host response to limit damage to the host, thus promoting disease tolerance and stimulating a resolutive response that restores homeostasis.
